title: Time & Space Complexity
objectives: Analyze loops to a Big-O bound
Always report both time and space

sections.markdown: Big-O describes how an algorithm's time or memory grows as input size n grows, ignoring constants and lower-order terms. It is the language of efficiency.
Big-O is about how a **recipe scales**, not how fast your stove is. O(n²) means doubling guests quadruples the work — regardless of how fast any single step runs.
Forgetting space complexity. A recursive solution may be O(n) time but O(n) stack space. Always state both.
Give complexity unprompted: 'This is O(n) time, O(1) space.' Then note worst vs average and whether a better bound exists.

flashcards.front: The Big-O ladder, best to worst?
flashcards.back: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2ⁿ) < O(n!).
O = upper bound (worst), Ω = lower bound (best), Θ = tight bound (both).

flashcards.front: How do nested vs sequential loops combine?
flashcards.back: Nested loops multiply their costs; sequential loops add.

quiz.q: Two nested loops over n give…
quiz.explain: Each level multiplies: n × n = n².

quiz.q: Which is fastest-growing (worst) for large n?
quiz.explain: Exponential growth dwarfs polynomial growth as n increases.
Drop constants and lower terms: O(n).

challenges.text: Given snippets, state the time and space complexity of each.
Rewrite an O(n²) duplicate-finder as O(n) with a hash set.
Find the k-th largest element in O(n) average with quickselect.
Solve a problem in O(1) extra space you first solved in O(n) (e.g. Floyd cycle detection).

interviewQuestions: Difference between O, Ω and Θ?
What's the complexity of binary search and why?
Average vs worst case for quicksort and hash lookups?
Reduce a given O(n²) solution to O(n log n) or O(n).
